name: Caching
explanation: Keeping a copy of data that is slow to fetch or compute, so later requests can be answered faster.
synonyms: cache;redis;cdn
triggers: faster;speed up;slow;store results;remember results;same request;expensive query;again and again;same query;recompute
requirements: Decide how fresh each piece of data must be, and set the expiry time to match;Invalidate or update cached data when the original changes;Never cache one user's private data where another user could receive it;Set Cache-Control headers for static files, and put a content hash in their names;Keep working, only slower, when the cache misses or is down;Cache by Cache-Control and real content type, never because a URL ends in .css or .js (cache deception)
done_when: Repeated requests are fast, and changes appear within the expected time;Users never see another user's data from the cache

name: Background jobs
explanation: Running slow tasks such as sending emails or generating reports outside the user's request, usually through a queue.
synonyms: job queue;task queue;worker;async jobs
triggers: in the background;send emails;takes too long;long running
requirements: Make jobs safe to run twice, because queues can deliver a job more than once;Retry failed jobs with growing delays and a maximum number of attempts;Move jobs that keep failing to a dead-letter queue, and alert someone;Pass ids to jobs rather than whole objects, and load fresh data inside the job;Show users the status of long jobs
done_when: A crashed worker does not lose jobs;Running the same job twice causes no duplicate emails or charges

name: Database migration
explanation: Versioned scripts that change a database schema step by step, so every environment stays in sync.
synonyms: schema migration;migrations;alembic;flyway
triggers: add a column;change the database;new table;rename a column;update the schema
requirements: Keep every schema change in a versioned migration file in the repository;Make changes backward compatible: add first, remove old columns in a later release;Test migrations on a copy with production-sized data;Avoid locking big tables for long, for example by creating indexes concurrently;Back up the database before risky migrations
done_when: Every environment reaches the same schema by running the migrations;The previous app version still works after the migration

name: Database index
explanation: A data structure that lets a database find rows quickly without scanning the whole table.
synonyms: index;b-tree index;query optimization
triggers: slow query;database is slow;search is slow;speed up queries;slow database;query is slow;query is very slow;query takes;table is slow;table is very slow;slow lookup
requirements: Index columns used in frequent WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY clauses;Check slow queries with EXPLAIN before and after adding an index;Order columns in combined indexes to match how queries filter;Remove unused indexes, because every index slows down writes;Use unique indexes where duplicates must never happen
done_when: The slow query uses the index and runs in milliseconds;Writes are not noticeably slower

name: Audit log
explanation: A permanent record of who did what and when, such as who changed a price or deleted a user, kept for security and accountability.
synonyms: audit trail;activity log;change history
triggers: who changed;who did;keep a record;history of changes;who deleted
requirements: Record who did what, when and from where for important actions;Make the log append-only, so entries cannot be changed or deleted;Never record passwords, tokens or full card numbers;Make entries searchable by user, record and date;Keep entries for as long as your rules or laws require
done_when: For any change to important data, you can find who made it and when;Neither users nor admins can edit or delete log entries

name: Soft delete
explanation: Marking a record as deleted instead of removing it, so it disappears from the app but can be restored later.
synonyms: trash;recycle bin;archive;deleted flag
triggers: restore deleted;recover deleted;recoverable;hide instead of delete;undelete;move to trash;deleted items
requirements: Add a deleted_at column instead of removing the row;Exclude deleted records from every normal query by default;Let users restore items within a stated time;Purge records for good after the retention period, or when the law requires it;Keep unique constraints for live rows, such as a partial unique index WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
done_when: Deleted items disappear everywhere but can be restored;Purged data is really gone after the retention period

name: Database transactions
explanation: Grouping several database changes so they all succeed or all fail together, keeping the data consistent.
synonyms: transaction;atomic operation;acid
triggers: all or nothing;both or neither;half saved;partially saved;money transfer
requirements: Wrap changes that must succeed together in one transaction;Keep transactions short, and do not call slow outside services inside them;Use row locks or a stricter isolation level where values can change at the same time;Retry on deadlocks and serialization failures;Use idempotency keys for payments and other actions that must not run twice
done_when: A failure halfway leaves no half-saved data;Two users changing the same data at once cannot corrupt it

name: Database backups
explanation: Regular copies of the database that can be restored after a mistake, an attack or a hardware failure.
synonyms: backup;point-in-time recovery;snapshot;disaster recovery
triggers: lose all data;restore the database;daily backup;copy of the database;if the server dies
requirements: Back up automatically on a schedule, with point-in-time recovery for important data;Store backups in a separate location or account;Encrypt backups and limit who can access them;Test restoring regularly;Alert when a backup fails
done_when: A test restore succeeds within the expected time;There is a backup for every day of the retention period

name: Scheduled jobs (cron)
explanation: Running a task automatically at fixed times or intervals, such as a nightly cleanup or a weekly report.
synonyms: cron;cron job;scheduler;recurring task;scheduled task
triggers: every night;every day;every hour;every week;every morning;at midnight;once a day;nightly
requirements: Make sure only one instance runs a job at a time, using a lock;Make jobs safe to rerun after a failure;Log each run, and alert when a job fails or does not run;Schedule in UTC, or handle time zones and daylight saving explicitly;Put a time limit on long jobs
done_when: A failed or missed run triggers an alert;Running two servers does not run the job twice

name: Retries with backoff
explanation: Automatically repeating a failed request after a growing delay, so brief outages fix themselves without overloading the server.
synonyms: retry;exponential backoff;retry logic;circuit breaker
triggers: try again;request again;server is busy;keeps failing;temporary error;flaky
requirements: Retry only temporary failures such as timeouts, 429 and 503, never 400 or 401;Wait longer after each attempt, with a little random jitter;Limit the number of attempts and the total time;Retry only safe or idempotent requests, or use idempotency keys;Respect the Retry-After header
done_when: A brief outage recovers without errors the user can see;A permanent error fails quickly instead of retrying forever

name: Error handling
explanation: Catching failures such as network errors, missing data or exceptions, and showing a helpful message instead of crashing.
synonyms: exception handling;try catch;error boundary;fallback ui
triggers: crash;app breaks;something went wrong;handle errors;white screen;if it fails
requirements: Show users a clear message and a way forward, never a raw stack trace;Catch errors at boundaries, such as React error boundaries and global server handlers;Log the full error with context for developers;Handle network errors, timeouts, empty data and invalid responses;Keep the user's input when an action fails
done_when: A failed request shows a helpful message and the app keeps working;Error details are logged but never shown to users

name: Cloud file storage
explanation: Storing uploaded files such as images and documents in a service like Amazon S3 or Cloudinary instead of the database, and serving them through a CDN.
synonyms: object storage;s3;blob storage;cloudinary
triggers: where to store files;store the images;store uploads;save files;host images
requirements: Keep storage buckets private and share files through short-lived signed URLs;Use generated file names instead of names supplied by users;Check file type and size before storing;Serve files through a CDN with caching;Delete files that are no longer referenced
done_when: Files cannot be listed or downloaded without permission;Large files are served quickly from the CDN

name: N+1 query problem (eager loading)
explanation: Code that runs one extra database query for every item in a list, for example one query for posts and then one more per post for its author. The fix is to load the related records in bulk with a join or a second batched query.
synonyms: n+1 queries;eager loading;select_related;prefetch_related;lazy loading queries;includes preload
triggers: page runs hundreds of queries;one query per row;too many database queries;list page is slow to load;load related records at once;query inside a loop
requirements: Count the queries each request runs in development and tests, not just its time;Load related records with a join or one IN query per relation, not one query per item;Eager load only the relations the page or response actually uses;Batch lookups in GraphQL resolvers and serializers, where per-item queries hide easily;Paginate the parent list so bulk loading stays bounded;Index the foreign key columns used to load related records
done_when: A list page runs a fixed number of queries whatever the number of items;A test fails if a known endpoint starts running more queries than expected;Response time stays flat as the list grows to a full page

name: Database connection pooling
explanation: Keeping a small set of open database connections and lending them to requests in turn, instead of opening a new connection each time. This stops the app from running out of the connections the database allows.
synonyms: connection pool;pgbouncer;pool size;db pool;connection pooler
triggers: too many connections error;database connection limit;reuse database connections;connections run out;serverless database connections;pool exhausted
requirements: Size pools so all app instances together stay below the database connection limit;Set a timeout for waiting on a free connection and return a clear error when it expires;Always return connections to the pool, also when a request fails;Use an external pooler when many processes or serverless functions connect;In transaction pooling mode avoid session state such as SET, LISTEN and session advisory locks;Check connections are still alive before reuse and recycle them periodically;Monitor active, idle and waiting connections
done_when: A load test at peak traffic never hits the database connection limit;Requests waiting for a connection fail fast with a clear error instead of hanging;No connections leak after errors in a long test run

name: Finding and analysing slow queries (EXPLAIN)
explanation: Finding which database queries use the most time, then reading their query plans to see why, such as a missing index or a full table scan.
synonyms: explain analyze;query plan;slow query log;pg_stat_statements;query profiling;execution plan
triggers: find slow queries;why is this query slow;which queries are slowest;query takes seconds;read a query plan;high database cpu
requirements: Rank queries by total time across all calls, not only by the slowest single call;Enable statement statistics or a slow query log with a sensible duration threshold;Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on realistic data volumes, since plans change with table size;EXPLAIN ANALYZE really runs the statement, so wrap writes in a transaction and roll back;Compare estimated and actual row counts and update statistics with ANALYZE when they differ;Look for sequential scans on large tables, nested loops over many rows and sorts spilling to disk;Re-measure after each change and keep the before and after plans
done_when: The top queries by total time are known and reviewed regularly;Each fixed query has a before and after plan showing the improvement;Slow queries are logged in production with their duration

name: Database constraints
explanation: Rules that the database itself enforces, such as unique values, required fields, allowed ranges and links between tables, so bad or inconsistent data can never be saved even if the app has a bug.
synonyms: foreign key;unique constraint;check constraint;not null constraint;referential integrity;on delete cascade
triggers: prevent duplicate rows;stop orphaned records;delete child rows automatically;field must not be empty in database;enforce valid values in database;broken links between tables
requirements: Mark columns NOT NULL unless a missing value has a real meaning;Add unique constraints for natural keys such as email or slug, not just app checks;Choose the on-delete behaviour of each foreign key on purpose: restrict, cascade or set null;Index foreign key columns yourself, since the database does not always do it automatically;Remember unique constraints treat NULLs as distinct unless configured otherwise;Translate constraint violations into clear user-facing errors, not server errors;Add constraints to big tables without long locks, for example create as not valid then validate
done_when: Inserting a duplicate or orphan row directly in SQL is rejected;Deleting a parent row behaves as designed for each foreign key;A constraint violation shows the user a clear message

name: Row locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE)
explanation: Locking the specific database rows you are about to change, so two requests cannot read and update the same record at the same time and overwrite each other.
synonyms: select for update;pessimistic locking;row lock;skip locked;for no key update
triggers: two users update same record;changes overwrite each other;stop double booking;prevent overselling stock;race condition in database;balance goes negative
requirements: Lock rows with SELECT FOR UPDATE inside the same transaction that changes them;Keep locking transactions short and never wait for user input or slow external calls while holding locks;Lock rows in a consistent order, such as by id, to avoid deadlocks;Retry the transaction when the database reports a deadlock or serialization failure;Use NOWAIT or a lock timeout where waiting is worse than failing;Use SKIP LOCKED for work queues so workers take different rows;Prefer a single conditional UPDATE when it can do the check and change at once
done_when: Two concurrent requests changing the same record never lose an update in a test;Deadlocks are retried and logged rather than shown as errors to users;No transaction holds row locks for more than a short time under load

name: Application locks (advisory or distributed locks)
explanation: Taking a named lock that is not tied to any table row, so only one process at a time runs a piece of work, such as a nightly report, a sync or a migration.
synonyms: advisory lock;distributed lock;mutex lock;named lock;pg_advisory_lock;lock key
triggers: only one instance runs the job;prevent the job running twice;stop overlapping cron runs;single runner across servers;job must not run in parallel
requirements: Derive a stable lock key from a clear name and document which code uses which key;Use a try-lock that returns at once when the lock is busy, unless waiting is intended;Prefer transaction-scoped locks, which release automatically on commit or rollback;Release session-scoped locks in a finally block, since they last until the session ends;Do not rely on session locks through a transaction-mode connection pooler;For locks outside the database, set an expiry and guard work against an expired lock
done_when: Starting the same job on two servers at once runs it only once;A crashed holder does not leave the lock taken forever;Lock waits and skipped runs are logged

name: Upsert (insert or update)
explanation: Inserting a row, or updating the existing one if it is already there, in one atomic database statement. This avoids duplicates when two requests try to create the same record at the same time.
synonyms: insert on conflict;insert or update;merge statement;on duplicate key update;insert or ignore
triggers: create if not exists;update if it already exists;avoid duplicate records on save;insert or replace row;sync records by external id
requirements: Back the upsert with a unique constraint or index on the matching columns;Do it in one statement, not a select followed by insert, which races under concurrency;Decide which columns the update may overwrite and which must keep their first value;Remember insert-or-ignore returns no row when nothing was inserted, so fetch it if needed;Deduplicate input rows first, since one statement cannot update the same row twice;Update timestamps such as updated_at in the update branch
done_when: Running the same upsert concurrently from many requests leaves exactly one row;Repeated runs give the same final data;The caller can tell whether a row was inserted or updated when it needs to

name: Bulk inserts and data loading
explanation: Writing large numbers of rows quickly by sending them in batches or with the database's bulk copy command, instead of one insert statement per row.
synonyms: bulk insert;batch insert;copy command;multi-row insert;bulk load
triggers: insert millions of rows;import is very slow;load a big csv into the database;speed up inserts;one insert per row is slow
requirements: Use the bulk copy command or multi-row inserts instead of one statement per row;Group many rows per transaction, with batches sized so a failure is cheap to retry;For very large first loads, add indexes and foreign keys after loading the data;Update planner statistics with ANALYZE after a large load;Validate and clean rows before loading and report rejected rows with their line numbers;Run large loads as background jobs and avoid locking tables users need
done_when: Loading a realistic large file finishes within the agreed time;Bad rows are reported without losing the good ones;Queries on the loaded table use good plans right after the load

name: Database seed data
explanation: Loading the starting data an app needs, such as default roles, countries or settings, plus optional demo data for development, in a repeatable script that is safe to run again.
synonyms: seed data;seeding;seed script;fixtures;reference data;sample data
triggers: default data on install;fill database with demo data;demo accounts for development;initial admin account;load list of countries
requirements: Make seeding idempotent so running it again does not create duplicates;Keep required reference data separate from demo or test data;Never load demo accounts or known passwords in production;Read initial admin credentials from secrets, not values in the code;Version seed data alongside migrations so it matches the schema;Keep seeded ids stable when other data or code refers to them
done_when: A fresh environment is usable after running migrations and seeds;Running the seed twice leaves the data unchanged;Production contains no demo users or sample records

name: Materialized views
explanation: Saving the result of a slow, expensive query as a stored table that can be read quickly, and refreshing it on a schedule or when needed.
synonyms: materialized view;precomputed table;summary table;refresh materialized view;rollup table
triggers: dashboard query is too slow;precompute report totals;store results of a heavy query;refresh stats every hour
requirements: Accept and show that the data can be stale, for example with a last refreshed time;Refresh on a schedule or after relevant changes, as a background job;Use a concurrent refresh so readers are not blocked, which needs a unique index;Add indexes to the materialized view for the queries that read it;Prevent overlapping refreshes and alert when a refresh fails;Measure refresh time as data grows, since a full refresh recomputes everything
done_when: Reads from the view are fast at production data size;Users can see how fresh the data is;A failed or slow refresh triggers an alert

name: Database triggers
explanation: Logic that the database runs automatically when rows are inserted, updated or deleted, for example to keep a timestamp, a counter or a history table up to date.
synonyms: database trigger;trigger function;before insert trigger;after update trigger;row trigger
triggers: update a column automatically on change;run code when a row changes;keep updated_at in sync;copy old row to history table
requirements: Keep trigger logic small, fast and free of external calls such as HTTP requests;Choose before triggers to change the row and after triggers to react to it;Prefer statement-level triggers for bulk changes when per-row work is not needed;Guard against triggers firing each other in loops;Remember some operations, such as truncate, do not fire row triggers;Keep triggers in version-controlled migrations and document them where developers will look;Test triggers with bulk updates to check their performance cost
done_when: Every trigger is defined in a migration and covered by a test;Bulk updates on triggered tables finish in acceptable time;Developers can find all triggers on a table from the docs

name: JSON columns in a relational database
explanation: Storing flexible, semi-structured data such as settings or extra attributes in a JSON column of a normal database table, and still being able to query and index it.
synonyms: jsonb;json column;json field;semi-structured data;document column
triggers: store flexible attributes;save settings as json;query inside json data;custom data per record;schemaless field in sql
requirements: Prefer the binary JSON type for querying and indexing over storing plain text;Keep fields that are filtered, joined or required as real columns;Validate the JSON shape in the app and with check constraints where possible;Index the JSON paths or keys that queries use, for example with a GIN or expression index;Version the structure and migrate old documents when it changes;Limit the document size to keep rows and updates fast
done_when: Queries on indexed JSON keys use the index;Invalid JSON shapes are rejected before saving;Old records still load after the structure changes

name: Primary keys and public IDs (UUID vs serial)
explanation: Choosing how each record is identified, such as auto-incrementing numbers or UUIDs, and deciding which identifiers are safe to show in URLs and APIs.
synonyms: uuid;uuidv7;auto increment id;identity column;surrogate key;public id;ulid
triggers: uuid or integer id;hide ids in urls;guessable record ids;sortable unique ids;generate ids before saving
requirements: Use standard identity columns for integer keys rather than older serial or hand-made counters;Prefer time-ordered UUIDs such as version 7 over random ones for index locality;Do not expose sequential ids publicly when counts or guessable ids would leak information;Never rely on an unguessable id as access control and always check permissions;Use one id type consistently in foreign keys, URLs and APIs;Use ids that can be generated outside the database when records are created offline or across shards
done_when: Public URLs do not reveal how many records exist;Changing an id in a URL to another user's record is refused;Inserts stay fast as the table grows large

name: Read replicas (read/write splitting)
explanation: Sending read-only queries to copies of the database called replicas, and writes to the main database, to spread the load. Replicas can lag slightly behind, which the app has to handle.
synonyms: read replica;read/write splitting;hot standby;replication lag;primary-replica;follower database
triggers: database overloaded with reads;send reads to a copy;scale database reads;user does not see their own change;stale data after saving
requirements: Send writes and reads that must be current, such as right after a save, to the primary;Read from the primary for a short time after a user writes, so they see their own change;Monitor replication lag and stop sending reads to a replica that falls too far behind;Expect long queries on a replica to be cancelled by replication conflicts and retry them;Keep transactions that mix reads and writes on the primary;Fall back to the primary if all replicas are unavailable
done_when: A user always sees their own change right after saving;Read traffic moves to replicas and primary load drops;A lagging replica is removed from rotation automatically

name: Table partitioning
explanation: Splitting one very large table into smaller pieces, for example one per month, while still querying it as a single table. Queries touch fewer rows and old data can be removed by dropping a whole piece.
synonyms: partitioning;partitioned table;range partitioning;list partitioning;hash partitioning;partition pruning
triggers: table has billions of rows;split table by month;delete old data quickly;huge events table is slow;archive old rows by date
requirements: Pick a partition key that most queries filter on, such as a date, so pruning works;Include the partition key in primary keys and unique constraints, as the database requires;Create future partitions ahead of time and alert if one is missing;Remove old data by detaching or dropping partitions instead of large deletes;Keep the partition count moderate, since too many partitions slow planning;Check with EXPLAIN that queries scan only the partitions they need
done_when: Queries filtered by the partition key scan only the matching partitions;Old data is removed in seconds by dropping a partition;Inserts never fail for lack of a partition

name: Query and transaction timeouts
explanation: Putting time limits on database statements, waits for locks and transactions left open, so one stuck or runaway query cannot block the rest of the app.
synonyms: statement timeout;lock timeout;idle in transaction timeout;query timeout;transaction timeout
triggers: query runs forever;database locked up;request hangs on database;kill long running queries;stuck open transaction
requirements: Set a statement timeout per role or connection for web requests, and a longer one for reports and jobs;Set a lock timeout, especially for migrations, so they fail instead of blocking all traffic;Set an idle-in-transaction timeout so forgotten transactions are ended;Avoid one global statement timeout for every session, which also cuts off maintenance work;Keep database timeouts shorter than the request timeout of the caller;Handle timeout errors with a clear message and log the query that hit the limit
done_when: A deliberately slow query is cancelled at the configured limit;A blocked migration fails quickly instead of stalling the app;Timeout errors appear in logs with the query involved

name: Storing trees and hierarchies in a database
explanation: Modelling nested data such as categories, folders, org charts or threaded replies in database tables, and querying a whole branch, its ancestors or its depth efficiently.
synonyms: adjacency list;recursive cte;with recursive;materialized path;closure table;nested sets;ltree
triggers: categories inside categories;parent and child records;threaded replies;org chart data;folder tree in database;get all subcategories
requirements: Store a parent id with a foreign key, and index it;Use recursive queries or a path column to fetch whole branches in one query;Prevent cycles, such as a node becoming its own ancestor, when moving nodes;Limit the depth the app accepts and that recursive queries will follow;Decide what happens to children when a parent is deleted;Keep stored paths or closure rows in sync in the same transaction as moves
done_when: A whole branch loads in one query;Moving a node under its own child is refused;Deleting a parent handles its children as designed

name: Geospatial queries (nearby search)
explanation: Storing locations as points or shapes and searching them by distance or area, such as finding stores within 5 km of the user, using spatial indexes to keep it fast.
synonyms: postgis;spatial index;geography type;radius search;geospatial database;gist index
triggers: find places near me;search within a radius;nearest store to user;locations inside an area;sort by distance
requirements: Store coordinates in a spatial type with a defined coordinate system, such as WGS 84;Keep longitude and latitude in the order the spatial functions expect, usually longitude first;Use a geography type or proper projection so distances are in metres, not degrees;Filter with an index-aware within-distance function, not by computing distance for every row;Add a spatial index on the location column;Limit and paginate results and cap the search radius
done_when: Nearby searches return correct results near the date line and the poles;Radius queries use the spatial index;Distances shown match a trusted map tool

name: Storing and calculating money
explanation: Storing amounts as exact decimals or as whole numbers of the smallest unit (such as cents) together with a currency code, and rounding correctly when calculating totals, tax and splits.
synonyms: currency amounts;decimal money;minor units;money type;monetary values
triggers: store prices in database;rounding errors in totals;cents in calculations;floating point price bug;split a bill evenly
requirements: Never use floating point types for money and store exact decimals or integer minor units;Store the ISO 4217 currency code with every amount;Do not assume two decimal places, since some currencies use zero or three;Round at defined steps with a documented rounding rule, not on every operation;When splitting amounts, give leftover minor units to some parts so the total still matches;Never add amounts in different currencies without an explicit conversion;Format amounts for display with the user's locale, separately from storage
done_when: Line items always add up exactly to the stored total;Zero-decimal currencies store and display correctly;Splitting 100 into 3 parts gives parts that sum to 100

name: Sequential document numbers (invoice numbering)
explanation: Generating human-readable numbers such as invoice numbers in strict order, without gaps where rules require it, even when many requests create documents at the same time.
synonyms: gapless sequence;invoice numbering;document numbering;sequential numbering;counter table
triggers: invoice numbers without gaps;next invoice number;numbers skip after errors;number per year;order numbers in sequence
requirements: Do not use database sequences for gapless numbers, since they skip values on rollback;Take the next number from a counter row locked in the same transaction that saves the document;Assign the number only when the document is finalised, not when a draft is created;Keep separate counters per series, such as per year or per company, if required;Add a unique constraint on the series and number;Cancel issued documents with a credit or void record instead of deleting them
done_when: Creating many documents concurrently gives unique numbers with no gaps;A failed save does not use up a number;Issued numbers are never reused or deleted

name: Case-insensitive lookups and uniqueness
explanation: Making values such as emails and usernames unique and findable regardless of upper or lower case, so Alice@example.com and alice@example.com count as the same account.
synonyms: citext;case insensitive unique;lower index;expression index;nondeterministic collation
triggers: email unique regardless of case;login with uppercase email;duplicate accounts different case;username capital letters
requirements: Enforce uniqueness in the database with a case-insensitive type or a unique index on the lowercased value;Use the same normalisation for lookups as for the unique index, so queries can use it;Trim surrounding spaces and apply Unicode normalisation before comparing;Keep the user's original casing for display if needed;Find existing duplicates that differ only by case before adding the constraint;Be aware that lowercasing rules differ by language for some letters
done_when: Signing up with an existing email in different case is refused;Logging in works whatever case the user types;Case-insensitive lookups use an index

name: Row-level security policies
explanation: Having the database itself limit which rows each user or tenant can read or change, so a missing filter in app code cannot leak another customer's data.
synonyms: rls;row security policy;row level security;database policies;tenant policies
triggers: users only see their own rows;tenant data isolation in database;restrict rows per customer;enforce access in sql
requirements: Enable row security on every table holding tenant or user data, and remember no policy means no rows;Write separate policies for reading and for writing new or changed rows;Force row security on each table, since the table owner bypasses it by default and superusers always do;Run the app as a role without bypass rights;Set the current user or tenant per transaction, so pooled connections do not leak it;Index the columns that policies filter on;Test with two tenants that each cannot see or change the other's rows
done_when: A query without a tenant filter still returns only the current tenant's rows;Inserting a row for another tenant is rejected;The app role cannot bypass row security

name: Graceful shutdown
explanation: Letting a server or worker that is asked to stop finish its in-flight requests and jobs, and close connections cleanly, instead of dying mid-work during deploys or scaling.
synonyms: graceful termination;sigterm handling;connection draining;drain mode
triggers: requests fail during deploy;finish work before stopping;server stops mid request;jobs lost on restart;handle stop signal
requirements: Handle the stop signal (SIGTERM) instead of exiting at once;Stop accepting new work and fail readiness checks so traffic moves elsewhere;Let in-flight requests finish, with a deadline shorter than the platform's kill timeout;Return unfinished jobs to the queue and make jobs safe to run again;Close database connections, flush logs and release locks before exiting;Log the start and end of shutdown and anything abandoned
done_when: A deploy under load causes no failed requests;Jobs interrupted by a restart run again and finish;The process exits before the platform has to force-kill it

name: Receiving and parsing inbound email
explanation: Accepting emails that people send to the app, such as replies to notifications or messages to a support address, and safely turning their text and attachments into data.
synonyms: inbound email;inbound parse;email parsing;reply by email;inbound mail routing;incoming mail webhook
triggers: reply to a notification by email;create ticket from email;forward emails into the app;process attachments from email;read emails sent to our app
requirements: Point the receiving domain or subdomain MX records at the mail service;Verify inbound webhook requests come from the provider;Do not trust the From header and check sender authentication results such as SPF and DKIM;Put a unique, hard-to-guess token in reply-to addresses to match replies to threads;Strip quoted earlier messages and signatures from replies;Treat HTML and attachments as untrusted, sanitise and scan them and limit sizes;Ignore auto-replies and bounces to avoid mail loops, and deduplicate by Message-ID
done_when: A reply by email appears in the right thread without the quoted text;Spoofed or unknown senders are rejected or flagged;The same email delivered twice is stored once

name: Email bounces and complaints
explanation: Processing notices that emails could not be delivered or were marked as spam, and keeping a suppression list so the app stops sending to those addresses and protects its sender reputation.

name: Data retention and expiry cleanup
explanation: Automatically deleting or archiving records once they are older than a set period, such as expired tokens, old logs or stale user data, so nothing is kept longer than needed.
synonyms: retention policy;data purging;ttl expiry;storage limitation;data lifecycle management
triggers: delete old records automatically;remove expired tokens;clear out old logs;keep data for 90 days;auto delete after a year;purge stale data;how long to keep data;old rows piling up
requirements: Write down a retention period and reason for each kind of data, including logs and backups;Run cleanup on a schedule and delete in small batches so locks and load stay low;Make the job safe to rerun and to resume after a crash partway through;For large time-based tables, drop or detach old partitions instead of bulk DELETE;Remember deleted data still lives in backups and replicas until they age out too;Support legal holds that pause deletion for specific records;Log how many records each run removed and alert when the job fails or stops running
